newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear woes expected to benefit LNG, coal.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear woes expected to benefit LNG, coal.

text.p: Coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG) stand to gain the most ground among replacement energy sources for Japan's electricity utilities as public opposition mounts to construction of new nuclear plants, analysts say.

Industry observers believe a series of recent accidents at facilities operated by the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) have partially derailed Japan's ambitious nuclear power development agenda.
The government-run PNC has experienced repeated radiation leakages over the last five years, many of which it did not report at the time.

And on March 11, PNC's nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in Tokaimura on the Pacific coast was the scene of Japan's worst-ever nuclear accident when an explosion exposed some 37 workers to low levels of radiation.
"Looking at the situation realistically, I don't think the construction of nuclear plants is going to move according to schedule," Tadatoshi Utaka, an analyst with Nikko Research Center said.

With Japanese electricity demand forecast to grow an annual 2.2 percent over the next nine years, any slowdown in Japan's nuclear power production would boost demand for hydro-carbon based power, analysts said.
"If there are going to be any changes...it will be a shift to LNG from nuclear energy," said Naoto Hashimoto, an analyst at Nomura Research Centre.
The meltdown of Japan's nuclear programme can be seen most vividly in discrepancies between targets for nuclear energy set by the government and those set by the industry, analysts said.
The government aims to raise the share of nuclear power to 42 percent of total electricity demand by 2010 from the current level of roughly 34 percent.

But in its latest 10-year programme released at the end of March, the Federation of Electric Power Companies (FEPC) estimated nuclear power would account for only 34.5 percent of electricity output in 2006.
Asked about the sluggish pace shown in the FEPC estimate, a Ministry of International Trade and Industry official acknowledged it showed the nation's nuclear power programme was behind schedule.
"It's becoming clear that the plan is not being implemented right on target, but we are still working to achieve it," the official said.

In the FEPC projection, oil-fired thermal power plants are expected to lose part of their share in the power pie, plunging to 9.8 percent in fiscal 2006/07, starting April, from 16.9 percent in fiscal 1996/97.
The FEPC forecast that the slack would be filled by coal-fired plants, which would grow to represent 20 percent of the total from 13.8 percent over the same period.
Although LNG's share would dip slightly to 22.9 percent from 23.1 percent, analysts said that LNG use would inevitably grow in the future, given that it burns more cleanly than coal.
"LNG could come to account for more than 40 percent of the energy used by utilities," Nomura's Hashimoto said.
Japan is already the world's biggest buyer of LNG.

The electricity industry is currently constructing three nuclear power plants which together will have the power to generate about 3.4 million kilowatts (kw) of electricity. The three plants are due to begin operating between July 1997 and January 2002.

It has plans to construct another four, with a total capacity of about 4.7 million kw, and to apply for the construction of a further five, with a total capacity of 6.9 million kw, within this fiscal year.
However, analysts predict that local opposition will delay construction of some of the plants.
